Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette: Ali, a 27-year-old Middle Eastern man and physical therapist, was assaulted one night while walking home from work. The event was sudden and unexpected: he heard footsteps behind him and turned to see a figure wearing cologne that overwhelmed his senses, followed by a violent attack. Since then, Ali has been struggling with the haunting memories of that night, particularly when exposed to similar triggers. The assault had left physical scars as well; the pain in his body serves as another potent reminder of what happened. Whenever he experiences physical discomfort or is near someone wearing cologne, Ali’s mind immediately flashes back to the traumatic event. The olfactory and somatic cues trigger a cascade of negative emotions, reinforcing his belief that he will never be able to feel normal again. This belief has left him feeling isolated from his wife and cautious in his interactions with patients. Ali had come to believe that he can't rely on himself anymore—a notion that is exacerbated each time he encounters a familiar scent or feels pain. These triggers not only remind him of the event but also reinforce his negative appraisals, making it increasingly difficult for him to trust his own judgment and reactions. What frightens Ali most is the constant fear that any reminder could bring back those feelings of helplessness. The sense of vulnerability has left him hyper-vigilant. He starts at unexpected movements or touch from others, reacting with alarm even in situations where there is no real threat. This startle response is a direct result of his negative appraisals and the constant fear that another attack could happen again. The more he feels threatened, the more he relies on maladaptive strategies like dissociation to cope. He often finds himself pretending that the event happened to someone else, which allows him to momentarily escape from the overwhelming emotions tied to the trauma. This dissociative behavior becomes a cycle; whenever Ali experiences a trigger, his mind immediately shifts away from reality, reinforcing the notion that he can't trust himself and amplifying his sense of threat. The maladaptive strategies also contribute to maintaining his triggers. By constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, Ali inadvertently keeps the memory of the assault alive. This hyper-focus on physical sensations only intensifies his startle response and heightens his overall state of alertness, making it increasingly difficult for him to relax. Ali’s work as a physical therapist has been affected by these symptoms. He avoids patients who wear cologne or have body positions that remind him of the attack. His avoidance behavior has strained his relationships with colleagues and patients alike, leading to a sense of isolation at work. The combination of negative appraisals, triggers, and maladaptive strategies has created a self-reinforcing cycle that feels almost inescapable. What finally brought Ali to seek help was an incident where he had a severe startle response during a therapy session with a patient wearing cologne, which led him to abruptly leave the room. He realized that his symptoms were interfering with his ability to function professionally and personally. Despite feeling ashamed of what happened to his body and fearing further attacks, Ali is most hopeful for finding ways to regain control over his life and rebuild trust in himself. Ali’s journey through trauma has left him grappling with a complex web of emotions and behaviors, but he remains determined to seek support and break the cycle that continues to torment him.
